text: Hans Muelich made 110 drawings of a duchess's jewels. In 1552 Albert V, Duke of Bavaria, ordered an inventory of the jewellery he and his wife owned, and the resulting Jewel Book of Duchess Anna is still in the Bavarian State Library. Muelich was the son of a Munich city painter. He studied with Barthel Beham, met Albrecht Altdorfer in Regensburg and travelled to Rome. Back in Munich he joined the painters' guild. He is best known for portraits of the city's leading families.

Aert van Waes lived and worked in Gouda but travelled in France and Italy to finish his training. He studied with Wouter Crabeth II, Reinier van Persijn and David Teniers the Younger. Houbraken says he learned etching from van Persijn and calls him a good draftsman. The same writer claims that van Waes and his friend Jan Govertsz Verbyl travelled together and both died of the same sudden sickness in 1649. The RKD disagrees and puts his death somewhere between 1664 and 1684.

Rigaud showed 155 works at the Royal Academy between 1772 and 1815. Decorative painting for lords such as Gower and Sefton paid him better. He was born in Turin to a Protestant merchant family of French descent and studied in Florence, Bologna and Rome. In Rome he became friends with the sculptor Johan Tobias Sergel and the painter James Barry. He reached London in 1771.

Most of Jules Veyrassat's pictures have animals in them. He studied with Henri Lehmann in Paris and showed at the Salon of 1848. Pierre Édouard Frère and Charles-François Daubigny pushed him toward etching, which he took up in the 1860s. He then worked with the critic Philip Gilbert Hamerton on two books, including Chapters on Animals. He seems never to have travelled abroad.

Niccolò dell'Abbate painted twelve frescoes in the Rocca di Scandiano, one for each book of the Aeneid. He was born in Modena, the son of a violinist, and trained in the studio of the sculptor Antonio Begarelli. Correggio and Parmigianino changed his style after he moved to Bologna. In 1552 he went to France and joined Francesco Primaticcio's team at Fontainebleau, part of the group now called the School of Fontainebleau that brought the Italian Renaissance to France.

Dirk Valkenburg went to Suriname to draw plants and birds. He travelled there in 1706 for Jonas Witsen, a wealthy Amsterdam city secretary who owned a plantation. Valkenburg had met Witsen through his teacher Michiel van Musscher. He also studied with Herman van Vollenhove and Jan Weenix. He worked in Vienna for the Prince of Liechtenstein too, and his paintings are mostly exotic landscapes, birds, and still lifes of fruit and flowers.

Gerrit Lundens ran an inn and traded wine as well as painting. He was born in Amsterdam, the son of a laundry bleacher, and may have trained with his brother-in-law Abraham van den Hecken. About 150 paintings are attributed to him, among them portraits, genre scenes and copies after old masters such as Rembrandt. He painted one vanitas. His wine business went bankrupt in 1671, and his last dated painting is from 1675.

None of Gijsbert van Veen's portrait paintings are known to have survived. He is remembered for reproductive engravings after other artists, such as his brother Otto. The Catholic family left Leiden for Antwerp in 1572 after the Dutch Revolt began. Gijsbert later worked in Brussels as an artist and a diplomat, and in 1603 he was paid for secret missions for the Archdukes Albert and Isabella. He made engravings in Rome and Venice, and from 1612 he lived in Antwerp.

The Duke of Marlborough liked Balthasar van den Bossche's work enough to commission a portrait of himself with a battle scene. Van den Bossche painted it together with Pieter van Bloemen, who was known for horses. He was born in Antwerp and studied under Gerard Thomas, who specialised in studio and picture gallery interiors. His own favourite subjects were picture galleries and artists' studios, like his master's. He spent some time in Paris, was back in Antwerp by 1700, and died there in 1715.

Male colleagues at first looked at Fré Cohen with suspicion, since she was a woman who also knew typesetting. In 1921 she designed ads for the Draka cable factory, and she later moved to a socialist publishing firm. She did most of the covers and page layouts for the socialist youth organisation AJC. Self-taught at first, she took lessons at the Quellinusschool and graduated with a Medal of Honor, the first the school ever gave. From 1929 to 1932 she worked for the Amsterdam city printing firm.

Apollonio di Giovanni ran a Florentine workshop that made wedding chests, called cassoni, and other furniture. He is also known as the Master of the Jarves Cassone. He worked with the woodworker Marco del Buono Giamberti, whose son became his pupil and heir. Their workshop is now credited with an illuminated golden tarot deck once called the Charles VI deck, which is usually named the Estensi deck today after the d'Este family that owned it. The Bibliothèque nationale de France holds its 17 remaining cards.

No signed work by Manfredi is documented. Several of the forty or so paintings now attributed to him were once thought to be by Caravaggio. He was born near Cremona and became one of the leading Caravaggisti. Manfredi, more than Caravaggio, popularised low-life genre painting among the next generation of followers. He painted for private clients rather than for public commissions, and collectors prized his work in the 17th century. French and Dutch painters who came to Italy learned Caravaggio's style largely through him.

Johann Gotthard von Müller prepared for the church before he turned to engraving. He studied under the court painter Guibal, then spent six years in Paris with the engraver Johann Wille and won several prizes. Duke Charles recalled him to Stuttgart in 1776 to teach, and Paris later summoned him to engrave a portrait of Louis XVI. His plate after Trumbull's Battle of Bunker Hill ranks next in importance. He became professor of engraving in Stuttgart and was knighted in 1818. He made 33 plates in all.

In 1880 Louis Apol joined an expedition to Spitsbergen on the SS Willem Barents, and the Arctic stayed with him as an inspiration for the rest of his life. He specialised in winter landscapes, mostly snowy forests with a bridge or fence, and people rarely appear in them. His father arranged private lessons when the talent showed early, and King Willem III gave him a scholarship in 1868. The Rijksmuseum and the Gemeentemuseum Den Haag hold his work. A street in Amsterdam bears his name.

Maurice Biais designed furniture and leather goods for La Maison Moderne, the art gallery founded by Julius Meier-Graefe. He began there in 1899. Besides that, he worked as a French painter, draughtsman and illustrator. He married Jane Avril in 1911, and the couple lived in Jouy-en-Josas until his death in 1926. People have attributed that death to his being gassed in World War I.

Paul Revere's midnight ride in 1775 made him a folk hero, but he earned his living as a silversmith and engraver. He was born in the North End of Boston and joined the Sons of Liberty. Longfellow's poem of 1861 turned the ride into legend. Revere later served as an officer in the Massachusetts Militia, and the Penobscot Expedition ended that service. After the war he went back to silversmithing and moved into casting bells and cannon. In 1800 he became the first American to roll copper into sheets for ships.

Shiba Kōkan is said to have boasted that he could forge Suzuki Harunobu perfectly. After Harunobu died in 1770, he signed some of his own prints with Harunobu's name, and they passed as genuine. He began at the Kanō school in Edo at 15 and left six years later. His ukiyo-e prints carry the name Harushige. As Kōkan he painted Western-style pictures in imitation of Dutch oils. He also took part in Western learning, especially astronomy.

Wyllie's father and his brother Lionel both painted, and both encouraged him to draw from an early age. He entered the Royal Academy Schools at 15 and studied under Edwin Landseer, John Everett Millais and Frederic Leighton. In 1869 he won the Turner Gold Medal. He went on to paint maritime scenes in oils and watercolours, and one description calls him the most distinguished marine artist of his day. His work is in the Tate, the Imperial War Museum and the National Maritime Museum.

Antonio d'Enrico, called Tanzio da Varallo, came from a hamlet in Alagna Valsesia. His two brothers were artists too. One painted frescoes, the other was a sculptor and architect. In 1600 a safe conduct let Melchiorre and Tanzio leave Valsesia to visit Rome for the Holy Year. His early altarpieces in Abruzzo show a debt to Caravaggio and to the severity of Spanish Caravaggism.

Zheng Xie resigned as a magistrate in Shandong after 12 years, reportedly following criticism for building a shelter for the poor. He had begun life in poverty and risen through the imperial examinations, but he refused to flatter senior officials. Afterwards he put his energy into art and became one of the Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou. Orchids, bamboo and stones were his best known subjects. His orchid drawings also shaped a new style of calligraphy.

Charles Henry Jeens engraved postage stamps for British colonies early in his career. He learned engraving from John Brain and William Greatbach, and he later made plates for The Art Journal. From about 1860 he worked with Macmillan and Co., for whom he produced many vignettes and portraits, including a series of Scientific Worthies in Nature. He died after a long illness in 1879 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Jacob Willemsz Delff the Younger won a well-paid commission to repair his grandfather's schutterstuk after the Delft Explosion damaged it in 1654. According to Houbraken, the job showed his respect for his grandfather and the value the Delft council placed on the painting. The picture now hangs in the Delft city hall, in the room reserved for weddings. The RKD adds that his wedding portrait and the pendant of his wife were drawn from lost paintings. The Leiden Library owns them.

Susanna at the Bath, painted in 1704, is among Jean-Baptiste Santerre's best known works. He was one of the first French painters to bring in Netherlandish influences. Santerre studied under the history painter Bon Boullogne and trained by copying old masters. His portraits sold well by the late 1690s, and he mixed the fantasy portrait of Rembrandt and Gerrit Dou with the allegorical portrait then fashionable in France. From 1715 until his death he painted for the Duke of Orléans.

Josef Eduard Teltscher was at Beethoven's deathbed. He was also close to Franz Schubert's circle of friends, and his portraits of Schubert are described as the most authentic. Born in Prague, he learned lithography in Brno and studied at the Vienna Academy from 1823. Contemporaries rated him as a miniaturist alongside Moritz Daffinger. He drowned in the port of Piraeus in 1837 on a study trip.

Leopold Loeffler's paintings were reproduced as lithographs and often reprinted in Polish magazines because of their references to national uprisings and battlefronts. He was born in Rzeszów under the Austrian partition, and his father moved the family to Lwów as a district secretary. He was a member of the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts from 1866. In 1877 Jan Matejko invited him to Kraków, where he became a professor at the School of Fine Arts. He kept painting until he died there in 1898.

Hans Burgkmair is credited with 834 woodcuts, most of them book illustrations. He was born in Augsburg, the son of the painter Thomas Burgkmair, and trained with Martin Schongauer in Colmar. Schongauer died before the training was finished. From about 1508 Burgkmair worked mostly on woodcut projects for Emperor Maximilian I. He made nearly half of the 135 prints in the Triumphs of Maximilian and most of the illustrations for Weisskunig. He visited Italy in 1507, which changed his style.

More than 700 portraits are attributed to Ezra Ames. He worked in Albany, New York. There he painted prominent people, including early portraits of Governor George Clinton and Alexander Hamilton. Nobody knows whether he had formal training. His account books show he also painted miniatures, carriages, fire buckets, fences, mirror frames and furniture. He was skilled at engraving too, and his portrait of Clinton won wide notice when it was shown at the Pennsylvania Academy in 1812.

Alfonso Parigi the Younger came from a family of architects: his father was Giulio and his grandfather Alfonso Parigi the Elder. He worked mainly in Florence and began very young as his father's assistant. After Giulio died in 1635, he became court architect to the Grand Dukes of Tuscany at the Palazzo Pitti. There he led the completion of the Boboli Gardens, building the Isolotto and the steps of the amphitheatre. He also worked on the Medici villas at Poggio a Caiano and Careggi.

Christina Robertson became the first honorary woman member of the Royal Scottish Academy in 1829. She was born in Kinghorn in Fife and trained with an uncle who painted miniatures. Soon she was earning more than he did, first from miniatures for Scottish patrons and later from oils and watercolours. She had her own studio by 1828, perhaps the first woman to do so. In Paris in the mid 1830s she met members of the Russian court, and she is remembered mostly for her portraits of the Russian imperial family.

Jacob Coning was one of the first painters in Denmark-Norway to specialise in topographical painting. He was born in The Hague, trained under his father Jacob Koninck and Adriaen van de Velde, and settled in Copenhagen in 1676. From 1680 he worked for the Danish court, possibly through his wife, who served Queen Charlotte Amalie. In 1698 he went to Norway to paint views for Frederiksberg Palace. Despite his court contacts he had money trouble and sometimes had to auction his paintings. He spent his last years in a poorhouse.

Jan van Ravenswaay grew up in Hilversum, where his father owned a cotton mill. He studied drawing with Jordanus Hoorn in Amersfoort and then took lessons from Pieter Gerardus van Os. After travelling in Belgium, Germany and Switzerland he joined the Royal Academy of Art in Amsterdam. A landscape of his won an honourable mention in a Felix Meritis competition in 1818. Among his pupils were Jacobus Theodorus Abels and Remigius Adrianus Haanen. His niece Adriana van Ravenswaay painted too.

Louis de Silvestre learned to draw from his father Israel, the King's Engraver, and later trained under Charles Le Brun and Bon Boullogne. In 1701 he went to Rome to study with Carlo Maratta. Back in Paris he entered the Académie de peinture et de sculpture in 1702 and became a professor in 1706. Later he was court painter to King Augustus II of Poland and director of the Royal Academy of Arts in Dresden. His older brother Louis the Elder was drawing-master to the Dauphin.

Mary Darly wrote, illustrated and published the first book on caricature drawing. A Book of Caricaturas, aimed at young gentlemen and ladies, appeared around 1762. Her husband Matthew began as a clockmaker's apprentice in 1735. He later ran print shops on the Strand that he always called the Acorn or the Golden Acorn, and he became famous for furniture designs and caricature. Once he put an etching of the miniature painter Richard Cosway in his window, titled the Macaroni Miniature Painter.

Napoléon Sarony's brother Oliver taught him portrait photography in Scarborough, England. Sarony had been born in Quebec City, moved to New York as a boy, and worked as an illustrator for Currier and Ives before starting a lithography firm in 1843. In 1858 he left that firm and spent eight years abroad. After returning to New York in 1866 he became a highly popular portrait photographer, best known for pictures of American theater stars. His son Otto continued the business.

Federico Zuccaro's parents sent him to Rome at 11 to study law, but he wanted to be an artist. He trained in the workshop of his elder brother Taddeo, a successful painter, and helped with its commissions. Around 1560 he joined a group working for Pope Pius IV at the Vatican, where he made decorations for the garden Casino and the History of Moses cycle. He later worked in Spain, France, the Spanish Netherlands and England. He is counted as an important representative of late Mannerism.

Frédéric Sorrieu imagined the nations of the world marching together past a tree of freedom. His series La République universelle démocratique et sociale had four gouache lithographs and presented forty-eight utopias. In one of them a procession of European nations, recognisable by their flags and costumes, passes a statue of the Republic. Christ, saints and angels watch from the heavens to stand for fraternity among nations. He was a French engraver and draughtsman known for works about the liberal and nationalist revolutions.

Ludvig Abelin Schou nearly quit painting after he failed to win a gold medal, and he thought of becoming a teacher or a clerk. A relative then gave him enough money to study in Italy. He reached Rome in 1864 and lived in nearby mountain villages for two years. Then he turned to classical themes and finished his best known picture, which shows Chione killed by Diana. In October 1866 he started travelling again and died of cholera in Florence. He had studied with Niels Simonsen and Wilhelm Marstrand.

Ludwig Dill started out in architecture at the Stuttgart Polytechnic and only moved to the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich in 1874. There he studied under Karl Theodor von Piloty, but the landscapes of Adolf Heinrich Lier influenced him more. The area around Venice, especially Chioggia, became a favourite for painting outdoors. He was a founding member of the Munich Secession and its president from 1894 to 1899. His friend Adolf Hölzel ran an art school in Dachau, and the moors and watercourses there drew Dill at once.

Balzac mentored Charles Albert d'Arnoux and advised him to sign his work Bertall, an anagram of his middle name. His family wanted him at the Ecole Polytechnique, but he studied painting in the studio of Michel Martin Drolling and then committed to illustration and caricature. He provided 3,600 drawings for Les Romans populaires illustrés, a series of 30 volumes published between 1849 and 1855. He also drew for magazines such as Le Magasin pittoresque, and he worked as an early photographer. He became the father of triplets in 1866.

A cannon shot killed Girolamo da Treviso at the Siege of Boulogne in 1544, where he was working as an engineer for Henry VIII. Giorgio Vasari writes that he went to England as a military engineer. He also painted there, and A Protestant Allegory in the Royal Collection shows the Pope on the ground, pelted with large stones. Earlier, in Bologna in the 1520s, he made sculptural decoration for the portal of San Petronio and grisaille paintings inside. His style followed Giorgione, with some influence of Raphael's St. Cecilia.

Godefroy Durand moved to London in 1869 to work full time for The Graphic, a newly founded illustrated weekly, where he became a special artist. He stayed with the paper for several decades. Born in Düsseldorf to French parents, he trained in Paris under Léon Cogniet and drew for leading French illustrated newspapers in the 1860s. In London he showed Un Coup de Canon at a benefit exhibition for French peasants hurt by the Franco-Prussian War. His watercolour of Montmartre during the siege of Paris was shown at the Royal Society of British Artists in 1873.

Gerhard von Kügelgen had a twin brother, Karl, who painted too. After school he studied painting in Koblenz, and from 1791 he worked in Bonn, where he painted the elector Maximilian Francis and other court figures. Archduke Maximilian paid for the brothers to travel as far as Riga. Gerhard later painted Goethe, Herder, Schiller and Caspar David Friedrich, among others. He became a professor at the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts. His son Wilhelm became a painter as well.

James Merritt Ives ran the business side of Currier and Ives, the print firm he co-managed with Nathaniel Currier. His father was superintendent of Bellevue Hospital in New York City. Ives went to work at 12 but kept educating himself in art by visiting galleries and the Astor Library. Currier's brother Charles recommended him, and Nathaniel hired him as a bookkeeper in 1852. His artistic knowledge gave him a feel for what the public wanted. He modernised the bookkeeping.

Paulus van Hillegaert painted landscapes, military scenes and equestrian portraits. His parents were Flemish immigrants, one from Leuven and one from Antwerp, and nobody knows with whom he trained. He may also have painted the figures in landscapes by Alexander Keirincx, who worked for a time in Amsterdam. His sons Francois and Paulus the Younger both became painters. Paulus the Younger died young in 1658. Cornelis de Bie wrote a commemorative poem about him.

William Henry Huddle's portrait of Davy Crockett hangs in the Texas State Capitol. The Texas State Legislature also commissioned him to paint official portraits of the state's chief executives, and he painted the surrender of Santa Anna. Born in Wytheville, Virginia, he served in the Confederate army before moving to Texas with his family. He trained at the National Academy of Design in New York and in Munich. He married the sculptor Nannie Carver in 1889 and died in 1892.

Antonio Gisbert painted important events from Spain's history in a realistic style, often with a political aim. He generally tried to promote liberal causes in his pictures. He began his studies at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando in Madrid in 1846, working under José de Madrazo. He directed the Museo del Prado from 1868 until 1873, when he resigned in opposition to the new First Spanish Republic. He then moved permanently to Paris and died there.

Only one work by Jacomart is documented, the Retable of Catì, a late collaboration with his follower Juan Rexach. Most of his life is scarcely documented. He worked in Valencia until Alfonso V of Aragon called him to Naples in 1442, and he influenced local artists there such as Colantonio. Later the king sent him to Italy again, and he met cardinal Alfonso Borgia, the future Pope Calixtus III. His style kept the influence of early Netherlandish painting instead of taking up the Italian Renaissance. He came back to Valencia for good in 1451.

Jan Rubczak's agent and patron was the poet and art dealer Léopold Zborowski. Rubczak studied at the Kraków Academy with Florian Cynk and Józef Pankiewicz, then in Leipzig and at the Académie Colarossi in Paris. He made many trips to Brittany and Normandy to paint coastal scenes. His etchings reached the Venice Biennale, and in Paris he ran his own drawing school. In 1924 he returned to newly independent Poland and taught there. He died at Auschwitz in 1942.

According to a colleague, Juan de Arellano chose to paint only flowers because the pay was better and the work was lighter. He was born in Santorcaz near Madrid, studied with Juan de Solís, and drew heavily on Flemish artists such as Daniel Seghers and Italians such as Mario Nuzzi. His Garland of Flowers, Birds and Butterfly is on display at the Louvre. He also painted for the sacristy of the church of San Jerónimo el Real in Madrid. The Prado has a good group of his still lifes.

Louis Tytgadt was one of six candidates allowed into the 1865 Prix de Rome competition for painting, but he did not win. He was a baker's son from Lovendegem and studied at the Ghent academy for twelve years. Afterwards he trained for two years in Alexandre Cabanel's studio in Paris. In Italy he made many sketches of local people and scenery. He visited the Frans Hals Museum in Haarlem with Eugène Fromentin. Later he taught at the Ghent academy, then directed it, and he chaired the museum committee of the city's Museum of Fine Arts.

Rafael Monleón joined the merchant marine and became a pilot after his studies in Valencia, and sailing around Europe gave him a talent for marine art. His father was an architect and a professor at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Carlos. Later he studied with Paul Jean Clays in Bruges and with Carlos de Haes. He painted shipwrecks and other dramatic scenes. He became conservator of the Museo Naval in Madrid in 1870. His treatise on the history of navigation and naval construction had over a thousand illustrations but went unpublished in his lifetime.

Reinhard Sebastian Zimmermann studied at the Munich Academy under Julius Schnorr, Heinrich Maria von Hess and Clemens von Zimmermann. At first he painted portraits. Then the Grand Duke of Baden appointed him royal painter, and he turned to Bavarian and Swabian peasant life. He repainted the same subject several times, such as Payment Difficulties, whose first version dates from 1852 and a later one from 1855. His paintings are in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and the Neue Pinakothek in Munich.

Louis de Moni studied the works of Gerard Dou and imitated the manner of Mieris. He was born in Breda, where he learned from Van Kessel and Biset. According to the RKD, he then attended the drawing academy in The Hague for several years and studied with Philip van Dyk. In 1726 he went with van Dyk to Cassel. Afterwards he settled in Leiden and died there in 1771. His portraits and genre scenes are simple and pleasing, though cold in colour.

Henry R. Robinson sold political caricatures from his print shop at 52 Courtland Street in New York City. He published mostly on political issues, was busiest between 1836 and 1840, and kept an office in Washington to follow federal affairs. He worked with artists such as Edward Williams Clay, and their collaboration made New York the centre of political cartooning in the United States. Lithograph shops like his were plentiful in the city in the 1840s. Most had a few printer's assistants and some boys who delivered the prints.

Born in Antwerp around 1590, Juan de la Corte worked in Spain as a painter of Flemish origin. He painted portraits and history subjects, but he excelled at battle scenes and perspective views. He also painted small pictures of sacred subjects. He served as painter to King Philip III, and Philip IV kept him in that post. Several of his pictures are in the palace of Buen Retiro. He died in Madrid in 1660.

Kikuchi Yōsai is best known for monochrome portraits of historical figures. He was the son of a samurai named Kawahara of Edo and was adopted by the Kikuchi family. At 18 he became a pupil of Takata Enjō, then studied the Kanō, Shijō and Maruyama schools and developed an independent style. For his illustrated history of Japanese heroes, the Zenken Kojitsu, he did extensive historical and even archaeological research. It shows over 500 major figures and was first printed as ten woodblock books in 1878.

David H. Forbes, author of a book on views of Hawaii, calls Lionel Walden the finest seascape painter to work there. Walden was born in Norwich, Connecticut, and first took an interest in art in Minnesota, where his father was rector of an Episcopal church. As a young man he studied painting in Paris with Carolus-Duran. He first visited Hawaii in 1911 and returned several times. Walden won medals from the Paris Salon and was made a Knight of the Legion of Honor before he died in Chantilly, France.

Pier Francesco became a priest at 25. He was the son of the Florentine painter Bartolomeo di Donato and had his first training in his father's workshop. He then joined the circle of Benozzo Gozzoli and worked with him in San Gimignano and Certaldo. In 1475 he worked with Domenico Ghirlandaio on the decoration of the nave of the Duomo of San Gimignano. He signed a Madonna and Saints in Sant'Agostino in San Gimignano in 1494, and a Tobias and the Angels in 1497.

Few prints by Shunshosai Hokucho survive. He worked in Osaka, and all of the images attributed to him are portraits of kabuki actors, many with yellow backgrounds. Such prints from Kyoto and Osaka are called Kamigata-e and were made almost entirely by amateur kabuki fans promoting their favourite actors. His prints also show the influence of Toyokuni I. What sets Hokucho apart is his wish to show the theatrical scene itself, even though the backgrounds are usually absent or only roughly realistic. He was active from 1822 to 1830.

In 1707 Bernard Lens became the first British artist to paint miniatures on ivory instead of vellum. Rosalba Carriera had invented watercolour on ivory in Venice around 1700. Lens served as miniature painter to George I and George II, and he taught miniature painting to Prince William and two princesses. Horace Walpole called him the incomparable painter in watercolours, though he lamented that the copies after great masters would not last. His son Peter Paul painted the portrait of him now in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

Frederick Mackenzie drew architecture almost exclusively. He was a pupil of the architect John Adey Repton and began making architectural and topographical drawings for the books of John Britton. His style was close to that of Auguste Pugin, with whom he worked. Of the 88 drawings he showed at the Water-colour Society, nearly all had English subjects. One of them records the original National Gallery, the former home of John Julius Angerstein, just before it was pulled down. He was the society's treasurer from 1831 until he died.

Marcellin Auzolle designed about fifty posters between 1890 and the 1930s. His 1896 poster for the Cinématographe Lumière seems to be the first of its kind for a film shown in a cinema. Born in Paris, he exhibited a portrait at the Salon des artistes français in 1887, under the name Marcel Auzolle. He is said to have been a pupil of Eugène Quignolot, probably in his well-known evening classes. He married Jeanne-Henriette L'Hermitte and died at home in Paris.

The Rijksmuseum owns an album of 331 pencil drawings by Willem Hendrik Schmidt. He taught himself to paint and then became a pupil of Jacob de Meijer. He worked in his father's business for some years, and only after his marriage did he give himself to painting full time. He began with genre and history scenes and later turned more to portraits. In 1842 he became a teacher at the academy in Delft that later grew into the technical university. His pupils included Christoffel Bisschop and Johannes Tavenraat.

Johann Wilhelm Meil made about 80 etchings after designs by Johann Michael Hoppenhaupt, among them work for the new palace at Sanssouci. He was the son of a court sculptor in Altenburg and taught himself painting in Leipzig. He came to Berlin in 1752 and also designed twelve vases for the terrace in front of the picture gallery at Sanssouci. For the Berlin court theatre he made costumes, and for the Royal Prussian porcelain manufactory he made designs. In 1801 he became director of the Prussian Academy of Arts, succeeding his own pupil Daniel Chodowiecki.

Constance-Marie Charpentier's husband was Georges Danton's brother-in-law. She took drawing lessons from Johann Georg Wille for ten years, then joined the studio of Jacques-Louis David, which accepted women beyond the quota the Academy set. Her painting La Mélancolie was remarkable because women painters usually stuck to still lifes, portraits and genre scenes, and the French state bought it in 1801. She won a gold medal at the Paris Salon in 1814. From 1821 she taught painting to women in her own studio.

Paul von Ravenstein married the youngest daughter of Moritz von Schwind in 1886. The son of a physician, he knew as a schoolboy that he wanted to paint, and the light and life of Italy thrilled him enough that he learned Italian. He began studying at the Karlsruhe art school in 1875, first under Hans Gude, whose naturalism shaped him, then under Gustav Schönleber, whose palette impressed him. He lived and worked in Karlsruhe, and the Grand Duke gave him the title of professor. He sometimes stayed at a holiday house in Villingen.

Henry Bright started out as a chemist's apprentice. His father, a watchmaker and jeweller in Saxmundham, placed him with a druggist in Woodbridge, and Bright drew on the side. In Norwich he worked for the chemist Paul Squires, an enthusiastic art collector who introduced him to the landscape painters of the Norwich School, including John Sell Cotman and John Berney Crome. Those meetings turned him to painting. In 1836 he went to London to study, and there he met David Cox and James Duffield Harding.

King Rama V of Siam bought Lucien Jonas's painting Les Rouffions, and it is still in the Royal Palace in Bangkok. Jonas grew up in Anzin in a northern family of industrialists and studied in Valenciennes, where he also learned the violin for seven years. He entered the École des beaux-arts in Paris in 1899 and later worked in Albert Maignan's studio. Henri Harpignies took to him and urged him to paint outdoors. A mining drama, Les Consolations, won him a silver medal at the Salon of 1905, the year he took the second Grand Prix de Rome.

Gustav Richter went to Egypt in 1861 for King Maximilian II of Bavaria to study the building of the pyramids, for a picture ordered for the Maximilianeum in Munich. In Constantinople he painted the portrait of Sultan Abdülaziz. He was the son of a Berlin master carpenter, studied under Eduard Holbein, and spent two years in Paris as a pupil of Léon Cogniet. From Rome he sent home many watercolours of Roman folk life. In the early 1870s he stayed at Livadia, the tsar's summer residence in Crimea, and painted Romanov family portraits there.

Louis-François Lejeune drew his famous Cossack on a lithographic stone in Alois Senefelder's workshop in Munich. His horses stood harnessed and waiting while a hundred proofs were printed, and he sent one to Napoleon. He is credited with much of lithography's arrival in France. Lejeune was a soldier first. He served as aide-de-camp to Marshal Berthier from 1800 to 1812, and in the Russian invasion he became brigade general and chief of staff to Davout.

Jules Verne mentions Adolphe Binet in his novel L'Île à hélice. Binet was a brother of Victor Binet and a pupil of Constant Troyon. He painted portraits and genre scenes. The best known are Le Paddock and Le Soir à Saint-Aubin-sur-Quillebeuf. He also worked on the decoration of the Seine prefect's office in the Paris city hall, and a sketch for it, dated 1889, is in the Petit Palais.

Alexandre Lacauchie grew up near the Porte Saint-Martin in Paris, where his mother ran the famous Café Flamand. He showed portraits, landscapes, pastels and drawings at the Salons from 1833 to 1835. His best known published work is the two-volume album Galerie des artistes dramatiques de Paris. It holds 80 full-length portraits. He often worked with the engraver Henri-Jules Faxardo, and his full-length portraits of Marceau and Kléber were engraved for a history of the French Revolution.

Johann Gottfried Auerbach painted portraits of Maria Theresa, Emperor Francis I and other Habsburgs. His huge equestrian portrait of Prince Eugene of Savoy is in the Museum of Military History in Vienna. Charles VI named him imperial court painter in 1735 and chamber painter in 1741. In Francesco Solimena's dedication picture for the emperor, Auerbach painted the portraits over heads that were already in place. They were stiff. Probably that suited the court's wish for ceremony.

Charles Billoin's great-grandson was the Belgian statesman Paul-Henri Spaak, counted among the Fathers of Europe. Billoin was the son of a cook in Brussels. He trained at the city's Royal Academy of Fine Arts. He painted history subjects, portraits and watercolours, and he also made etchings and lithographs. At the Brussels Salon of 1845 he won a silver-gilt medal for his watercolour L'Invention de la Sainte-croix, and he showed the lithograph Laure et Pétrarque and two portraits from life there too.

Johannes Stradanus designed tapestries, prints and pottery as well as painting altarpieces. He was born in Bruges. He trained with his father and then with the genre painter Pieter Aertsen in Antwerp. After travelling through Lyon and Venice he settled in Florence, where he became a prominent court artist to the Medici. Print publishers across Europe circulated his designs for centuries. He lived in Naples from 1576 until about 1580 and died in Florence in 1605.

Theodore Poulakis is considered the father of the Heptanese school. Born in Chania on Crete, he was living in Venice by the age of 24 and stayed thirteen years. There he belonged to the Greek Brotherhood of Venice, in the company of Cretan painters such as Emmanuel Tzanes. In 1657 he moved to Corfu, where he signed a six-year contract to teach painting to Tzorzi, the son of Marinos Damistras. Over 130 of his paintings have survived. They show qualities of the Venetian school.
